match.reason: None of the bank points teaches how individuals can volunteer, fundraise, advocate or make ethical choices for global health; they cover health promotion, SDGs, inequities and resources, which are different ideas.

draft.title: Taking action for global health
card: Individuals can support health and human development in other countries as well as their own. There are four common ways to take action.
Volunteer
give time or skills to a cause, such as helping at a charity's local event. Fundraise: raise money for a cause, such as a fun run where the money goes to a health program.
Advocate
speak up to change minds or policy, such as writing to a member of parliament about clean water.
Ethical choices
choose products and services that treat workers fairly and cause less harm, such as buying fair trade goods.
draft.remember: Individuals can act by giving time, raising money, speaking up or choosing carefully what they buy.

a.q: Priya writes to her local member of parliament, asking the government to put more funding into clean water programs overseas. Which type of action is this?
a.why: Priya is speaking up to try to change a policy, which is advocacy. It is not fundraising, because she is not raising money herself. It is also not volunteering, because she is not giving her time to a project.
a.clue: She is trying to change what the government does.

b.q: Tom's class holds a cake stall and sends all the money to a charity that funds childhood vaccines. Which type of action is this?
b.why: The class is raising money for a health program, which is fundraising. Running the stall takes time and effort, so volunteering is tempting. But the aim is to raise money, and the action is named after that aim.
b.clue: Think about what the stall produces for the charity.

problems.detail: The card's volunteering example, 'helping at a charity's local event', is very close to a class running a cake stall for a charity. A student could reasonably argue for Volunteering. The why settles this with a rule, 'the action is named after that aim', which the card never teaches. The card or question should make clear that money raised for the cause makes it fundraising.

check.summary: Both questions have clear intended answers (Advocating, Fundraising). In question b, the card's volunteering example overlaps with running a cake stall, and the why relies on a naming rule the card does not teach.

proposal.title: Taking action for global health
card: Volunteer
give your time or skills directly to a cause, such as helping at a health clinic or teaching first aid. The help given is the time itself.
Fundraise
raise money for a cause, such as a fun run or a sausage sizzle. If an event raises money for the cause, it is fundraising, even though people give time to run it.
Advocate
speak up to change minds or policy, such as writing to a member of parliament about clean water programs overseas.
Ethical choices
choose products and services that treat workers fairly and cause less harm, such as buying fair trade goods.
proposal.remember: Individuals can support health and human development by giving time, raising money, speaking up or choosing carefully what they buy.
